fight: Is a generic global GMPE with a single Vs30 adequate for Nepal earthquake scenarios, or do Kathmandu basin effects and Himalaya-specific attenuation dominate?

side_a.position: Generic NGA-West2 style model (the Atlas uses BSSA14) with Vs30 scaling gives defensible first-order PGA bands

side_b.position: Gorkha records show Himalaya-specific relations fit better and Kathmandu basin long-period amplification (~0.4 s, ~5 s) far exceeds code spectra; rock-only PGA misstates demand

evidence_quality_delta: Side B is empirical (measured Gorkha strong motion); side A is a modelling convention
scope_overlap: Partly scoped: PGA bands may be adequate regionally but wrong in the Kathmandu basin and for long-period structures

fight: Should GLOF scenario origins follow the official potentially-dangerous-lake list, or does the 2024 Thame cascade show that list misses the real hazards?

side_a.position: ICIMOD 2020 inventory ranks 21 Nepal PDGLs on lake, dam, glacier and surroundings criteria

side_b.position: Thame 2024 came from two small lakes not on any danger list; triggers excluded by the PDGL criteria (seismic, cascades) matter

evidence_quality_delta: Side B is a single well-documented event against a systematic inventory; both empirical
scope_overlap: Genuine: list-based origin selection under-represents cascade and small-lake hazards

fight: Can a constant-celerity hydrograph routing give useful flood/GLOF arrival times, or are sediment-laden process chains too different?

side_a.position: Simple kinematic or celerity-based routing is transparent and fast; Palcacocha back-calculation gives 36-70 min travel ranges usable as bounds

side_b.position: Local-inertia routing raises peak NSE 0.48 to 0.71; Melamchi and Thame moved massive sediment (aggradation 5-20 m); Tsho Rolpa breach peaks span 8,198-26,662 m3/s

evidence_quality_delta: Side B is stronger (measured and benchmarked), but side A is defensible if framed as a wide range
scope_overlap: Scoped: simple routing is fine as an explicitly uncertain range, not as a single arrival time

fight: Has Nepal's flood early warning succeeded, or does it still fail at the last mile?

side_a.position: Flood deaths fell from 166 (2017) to 27 (2022) after FFEWS and SMS; Ncell sent 4.4 million alerts in 2023; BRCHP upgraded 158 stations and radar

side_b.position: Sept 2024: accurate four-day alert yet ~250 deaths; 2026 Bhotekoshi: generic Nepali-only SMS, 16-minute cross-border gap, Facebook post 5 h later; SMS manual and congestion-prone

evidence_quality_delta: Side A uses agency/operator self-reporting; side B mixes journalism and a scoping review
scope_overlap: Both right: riverine forecasting improved; urban flash floods, GLOFs and transboundary events still fail at dissemination

fight: Is SMS enough, or should Nepal's alerts move to CAP and cell broadcast (and should the Atlas plan for that)?

side_a.position: SMS via NTC/Ncell is established since 2016 and reaching millions; a voice-call pilot started in 2025

side_b.position: CAP adopted by WMO (2023) and Nepal agreed to an implementation plan (Apr 2025); cell broadcast costed at $1.75-3M but not procured

scope_overlap: Sequential, not opposed: SMS now, CAP in planning; no public CAP feed found yet

side_a.position: MICS 2024/25: 82% of households have internet (rural 73%, Karnali 68.5%)

side_b.position: ITU IDI 2026: 48.4% of individuals use the internet; DataReportal: 55.8%

scope_overlap: Scoped: household access vs individual use; both imply a large offline and low-bandwidth minority

fight: Can an open disaster-data platform become self-sustaining?

side_a.position: GeoNode became self-sustaining via its open-source community, ~200% ROI

side_b.position: No OpenDRI project built a self-sustaining revenue stream; data goes stale without continuous funding

evidence_quality_delta: Both GFDRR self-reporting; no independent evaluation
scope_overlap: Scoped: software can sustain via a community; data currency and country platforms do not

fight: How should uncertainty be shown to the public?

side_a.position: Natural-frequency formats and isarithmic maps improve comprehension

side_b.position: Benefit fades for low-probability high-consequence events; hard map boundaries carry legal and political weight and false reassurance can kill (L'Aquila)

scope_overlap: Complementary: show ranges and gradients, avoid crisp safe/unsafe lines
